evidence_ref: `go test ./internal/broker/verify/ -count=1` → ok, 92.8% coverage · `ladder_test.go` (17 tests, incl. `TestLadderPropertiesHoldOverEveryAcceptedHistory`) · **mutation run: 11 mutants via `dev/mutate.sh`, 9 killed, 2 allowlisted as proven-derived** · `make -C k8s-operator test` all suites green · L0 18/18 · `invariants-gate.py` 15/15

Nine died. The two that survived are the two the check names most explicitly — "at most one rung-2 alternative" and "never restarts at rung 1 after a rollback" — and the reason is not a missing test: **within a chain-valid history they are logically unreachable.** Monotonicity plus the no-self-transition rule already make each rung enterable at most once, so both `if`s are derived, and every negative-control history written to poke them also descended, letting the monotonicity rule fire first. Both derived rules are **kept**, with the finding written into `ladder.go` — the implication runs one way, so if a future spec revision relaxes monotonicity they stop being derived and become the only thing enforcing the bound, and a rule deleted for redundancy is a rule nobody restores when the premise changes. **The L2 instance is open and is not recorded here.**
